title: I. Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov
section: Book I — The History Of A Family
paragraphs: Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov was the third son of Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, a landowner well known in our district in his own day, and still remembered among us because of his grim and tragic death, which happened thirteen years ago, and which I'll describe in its proper place. For now I'll only say that this "landowner"—for that's what we used to call him, though he barely spent a day of his life on his own estate—was a strange character, yet one fairly common: a type that was abject and vicious and at the same time senseless. But he was one of those senseless people who are perfectly capable of managing their worldly affairs, and, it seems, nothing else. Fyodor Pavlovitch, for instance, began with almost nothing; his estate was tiny; he ran around dining at other men's tables and attached himself to them as a hanger-on, yet when he died it turned out he had a hundred thousand roubles in hard cash. At the same time, he was all his life one of the most senseless, absurd fellows in the whole district. I repeat, it wasn't stupidity—most of these absurd fellows are shrewd and intelligent enough—but pure senselessness, and a peculiarly Russian brand of it.

He was married twice and had three sons: the eldest, Dmitri, by his first wife, and two more, Ivan and Alexey, by his second. Fyodor Pavlovitch's first wife, Adelaïda Ivanovna, belonged to a fairly rich and distinguished noble family, the Miüsovs, who were also landowners in our district. How it came about that an heiress—a beauty, and on top of that one of those spirited, intelligent young women so common in this generation but occasionally found in the last—could have married such a worthless, puny weakling, as we all called him, I won't even try to explain. I once knew a young lady of the last "romantic" generation who, after several years of an enigmatic passion for a gentleman whom she could easily have married at any moment, invented insurmountable obstacles to their union, and ended up throwing herself one stormy night from a high bank—almost a cliff—into a deep and rushing river, perishing purely to satisfy her own whim, and to imitate Shakespeare's Ophelia. If that cliff, her chosen and favorite spot, had been less picturesque, if a prosaic flat bank had stood in its place, the suicide would most likely never have happened. This is a fact, and there have probably been more than a few similar cases in the last two or three generations. Adelaïda Ivanovna Miüsov's action was, no doubt, a similar echo of other people's ideas, born of the irritation caused by a lack of mental freedom. She wanted, perhaps, to assert her feminine independence, to defy class distinctions and the despotism of her family. And a pliable imagination persuaded her, we must suppose, for one brief moment, that Fyodor Pavlovitch, despite his parasitic status, was one of the bold and ironic spirits of that progressive age—though he was in fact nothing more than an ill-tempered buffoon. What gave the marriage its flavor was that it was preceded by an elopement, and this greatly captivated Adelaïda Ivanovna's imagination. Fyodor Pavlovitch's situation at the time made him unusually eager for any such adventure, since he was desperate to make his way in the world one way or another. Attaching himself to a good family and getting his hands on a dowry was a tempting prospect. As for mutual love, it apparently didn't exist, either in the bride or in him, despite Adelaïda Ivanovna's beauty. This was perhaps a unique episode in the life of Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was always of a voluptuous temperament and ready to chase any skirt on the slightest encouragement. She seems to have been the only woman who made no particular impression on his senses.

Right after the elopement Adelaïda Ivanovna realized in a flash that she felt nothing for her husband but contempt. So the marriage showed its true colors with extraordinary speed. Although the family accepted the event pretty quickly and handed over the runaway bride's dowry, husband and wife began to lead a thoroughly disorderly life, and there were endless quarrels between them. It was said that the young wife showed incomparably more generosity and dignity than Fyodor Pavlovitch, who, as is now known, got hold of all her money—up to twenty-five thousand roubles—as soon as she received it, so that those thousands were lost to her forever. The little village and the rather fine town house that were part of her dowry he did his utmost for a long time to transfer into his own name by means of some deed of conveyance. He would probably have succeeded, simply through her moral exhaustion and her desire to be rid of him, and from the contempt and loathing his persistent, shameless badgering stirred in her. But fortunately Adelaïda Ivanovna's family stepped in and thwarted his greed. It's known for a fact that frequent fights broke out between husband and wife, but rumor had it that Fyodor Pavlovitch did not beat his wife—she beat him, for she was a hot-tempered, bold, dark-browed, impatient woman of remarkable physical strength. Finally she left the house and ran off from Fyodor Pavlovitch with a penniless divinity student, leaving Mitya, a child of three, in her husband's hands. Immediately Fyodor Pavlovitch introduced a regular harem into the house and gave himself over to drunken orgies. In between, he drove all over the province, tearfully complaining to everyone about Adelaïda Ivanovna having left him, going into details too disgraceful for a husband to mention about his own married life. What seemed to gratify him most and flatter his self-love was to play the ridiculous role of the injured husband and parade his suffering with embellishments.

"Fyodor Pavlovitch, one would think you'd just gotten a promotion, you look so pleased in spite of your sorrow," the scoffers said to him. Many even added that he was delighted by this new comic part in which to play the buffoon, and that he pretended to be unaware of his absurd position simply to make it funnier. But who knows—maybe it was genuine simplicity. At last he managed to track down his runaway wife. The poor woman turned out to be in Petersburg, where she had gone with her divinity student and had thrown herself into a life of complete emancipation. Fyodor Pavlovitch at once began bustling about, making preparations to go to Petersburg—for what purpose he couldn't have said himself. He might actually have gone; but having decided on the trip, he felt immediately entitled to fortify himself for the journey with another bout of reckless drinking. And just at that moment his wife's family received news of her death in Petersburg. She had died quite suddenly in a garret, according to one story, of typhus, or, as another version had it, of starvation. Fyodor Pavlovitch was drunk when he heard of his wife's death, and the story goes that he ran out into the street and began shouting with joy, raising his hands to heaven: "Lord, now lettest Thou Thy servant depart in peace," but others say he wept uncontrollably like a little child, so much so that people felt sorry for him despite the repulsion he inspired. It's entirely possible that both versions were true—that he rejoiced at his release and at the same time wept for the one who had released him. As a rule, people, even the wicked, are far more naïve and simple-hearted than we imagine. And so are we ourselves.
